findings.title: Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive, so blocks are trivially bypassed
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact `where(email: email)` lookup, and the signup flow stores emails exactly as typed: `User.new_from_params` assigns `params[:email]` raw, the User model has no email downcasing callback, and the email uniqueness validator plus the Postgres unique index on users.email are both case-sensitive. Blocking `spammer@example.com` therefore does nothing to stop `Spammer@example.com` or `SPAMMER@example.com` from registering — the lookup misses the row and a separate account is created. The block should normalize case (store emails lowercase and compare against `email.downcase`) to be effective as an anti-abuse control.

findings.title: Validator performs DB writes during validation; match_count is double-counted per signup
findings.body: validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which as a side effect increments match_count and sets last_match_at on the blocked_emails row. Validation is normally read-only, and here it runs more than once per signup: UsersController#create calls `user.valid?` at line 168 (before the DiscourseHub check) and then `user.save` at line 172, which validates again — so one blocked signup attempt records two matches. Any other `user.valid?`/`save` with a changed email (including records that fail for unrelated reasons or are rolled back) also bumps the counters, so match_count cannot be trusted as a count of signup attempts. The stats update should happen once, at the point the signup is actually rejected, not inside the validator.

findings.title: match_count increment is a read-modify-write and loses updates under concurrency
findings.body: In BlockedEmail.should_block?, `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` reads the counter into memory and writes it back. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email both read the same value, so one increment is silently lost. Use an atomic update instead, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...")` or `update_counters`, which also avoids re-running validations and callbacks for a stats update.

findings.title: rejectedEmails array is defined on the prototype and shared across instances
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` in the hash passed to `Discourse.Controller.extend` puts a single mutable array on the controller's prototype, shared by every instance. The app currently instantiates this controller once, but any second instantiation — in JS tests, or if the controller is torn down and recreated — inherits emails rejected during earlier usage, and mutations via `pushObject` leak between instances. Initialize it per-instance instead, e.g. in an `init()` override with `this.set('rejectedEmails', Em.A([]))`.

findings.title: No test covers the new errors/values response contract the client depends on
findings.body: The failed-signup JSON now includes `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`, and the new client behavior — pushing `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` only when `result.errors.email` is present — depends on both keys existing with exactly these shapes. No controller/request spec (or JS test) was added for this contract, so a rename or a change in how errors are serialized would silently break the "prevent resubmitting a blocked email" flow without any failing test.
